parakeet: The resurrection argument is a non sequitur sustained by hidden premises, an interpretive leap disguised as a proof. The argument is often circular because Christians use scripture to validate the resurrection, then use the resurrection to validate scripture. They say the resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God because Scripture says so, and Scripture is trustworthy because Jesus rose, and we know he rose because Scripture says so. That's not independent proof, that's a closed loop. It's a system of reinforcing itself by appealing back to its own internal claims. That's why Christians often treat the resurrection as proof when it's really functioning more like interpretation layered onto a claim. The framework is already in place, the text is already trusted, and the conclusion is already favored. The resurrection is then used not to establish the framework from scratch, but to confirm what the framework has already taught people to believe. The resurrection argument is a non-sequitur sustained by hidden premises, an interpretive leap disguised as a proof. An alleged event is being asked to establish an entire theological framework that must already be assumed in order for the event to have that meaning. How does an empty tomb mean God exists? How does a resurrection claim mean that this is the Son of God? How does someone returning to life mean atonement is true? How does an unusual event mean Christian theology wins over every competing explanation until those questions are answered without appealing back to the same assumed framework? The resurrection is not functioning as proof. It's functioning as a conclusion people have already been taught to see in the event. That is one of the biggest leaps in the resurrection argument. Because even if something strange or unusual happened, you would still not know what caused it, what it meant, whether the story was reported accurately, or whether the theological conclusion being drawn from it actually matched the event itself. That's the difference between an anomaly and a doctrine. An anomaly is an unusual event. A doctrine is a highly specific interpretive conclusion about reality, meaning, purpose, and truth. The distance between those two things is enormous. To move from one to the other requires argument, evidence, and justification. It cannot be done honestly by treating the event itself as if it already contains the full theological system inside it.
